agents.stance: PRAGMATIST: practical, resource-aware, shippable. Favor ideas that a small team could start on Monday. Prefer clarity and feasibility over cleverness.
CONTRARIAN: challenge the obvious. Invert the default assumption, argue the opposite of the expected move, and surface what everyone is ignoring.
DOMAIN-EXPERT: a deep specialist. Apply hard-won craft knowledge and non-obvious best practice; cite the mechanism, not just the vibe.
OUTSIDER-ANALOGY: import a mechanism from an unrelated field (biology, logistics, games, nature) and reason by analogy into this problem.
VISIONARY: aim for 10x, not 10%. Describe the ambitious end-state and work backward to a bold first move.

candidates.text: Run a weekly 30-minute user interview sprint with 3-5 existing customers, recording what problems they mention unprompted. Rotate who conducts interviews and tally recurring pain points across 4 weeks to identify the top 3 build candidates.

Deploy a simple in-app survey (2-3 questions max) asking users what feature would save them the most time this month, then ship the top-voted feature within a sprint. Repeat monthly to build a feedback loop.

Analyze your support/help tickets and community posts from the last 90 days, categorizing requests by frequency and effort-to-build. Pick the highest-frequency, lowest-effort item as your next project.

Have each team member spend 2 hours independently using a competitor's product or adjacent tool, then share one feature observation that surprised them. Build whichever idea gets the most team enthusiasm after these quick research sessions.

Commit to building one small feature each week for the next month based on the team's own frustrations using the product, without waiting for external data. Measure adoption internally to see which resonates, then double down on the winner.

Set up a daily Slack bot that pulls one random user message or piece of feedback from your last month of data and posts it for team discussion. After 20 days, identify which themes appeared most and tackle the clearest pattern.

Build nothing new and instead charge users for deeper access to existing features—treat the backlog as a pricing lever rather than a roadmap. This reveals what users actually value by forcing them to vote with money, eliminating the gap between stated wants and real demand.

Deliberately build the opposite of what users request. Frame it as an experiment: if users hate it, you've learned their true preferences through resistance rather than through unreliable surveys. If they adapt, you've discovered they're wrong about what they need.

Assign each team member a different user segment and have them compete to justify building a feature that only their segment would use—winner gets built. This surfaces the hidden priority conflicts within your user base instead of averaging them into mediocrity.

Randomly select 20% of paying users and give them the opposite of what they ask for; track their churn and engagement against the control group. Use churn as signal: if they don't leave, you've found unlocked value; if they do, you've confirmed their stated preference.

Ban all user interviews and surveys for one sprint. Instead, obsess over the 1% of users who engage obsessively with a single feature and reverse-engineer why that feature matters to them—they may represent a future market segment worth serving before it becomes obvious.

Let your competitors' roadmaps drive your decision: build the inverse of what they're building. Assume they have better user data than you, so by moving opposite you own an underserved position and force them to follow you instead of chasing their lead.

Run a Jobs-to-be-Done interview study with 12-15 recent users who chose your product over alternatives, focusing on the progress they were trying to make rather than feature requests. This reveals decision logic and unmet needs that surveys miss because users can't articulate what they don't know exists.

Instrument your product with event-driven telemetry that tracks the ratio of feature adoption-to-churn: which features correlate with users staying versus leaving? Prioritize building adjacent features near high-adoption clusters, since you're riding existing user behavior rather than predicting demand.

Identify your power users (top 5-10% by engagement) and embed someone on their team for a week to watch work in situ; their workarounds and hacks signal real friction points that matter enough to create shadow processes. This is harder to fake than what power users will tell you in a meeting.

Deploy a fake-door test: add incomplete UI elements or landing pages for speculative features and measure click-through rates and time-to-bounce. The cost is near-zero and you learn which feature directions generate spontaneous intent rather than retrofitting demand onto what you've already built.

Track the linguistic patterns in support tickets and user communities using topic modeling to find clusters of repeated problems that your product doesn't address—these are high-frequency, real enough that users are spending time describing them, and already partially characterized.

Run a forced-trade-off exercise where users allocate a fixed budget of points across a pre-defined set of potential features or improvements; this avoids the "yes to everything" bias of open feedback and reveals what users actually deprioritize when forced to choose, signaling true value.

Apply ecological succession modeling: treat user needs like pioneer vs. climax species—start by shipping the simplest feature that attracts early adopters (pioneer), then progressively add features that create conditions for more sophisticated user needs (succession). Use engagement patterns to detect when the ecosystem is ready for the next layer.

Adopt a venture capital portfolio approach: build 3-5 small, low-cost prototypes in parallel targeting different user hypotheses, run them for a fixed sprint, then double down on the one with the best early traction metrics. Treat each prototype as a seed-stage bet rather than betting the whole round on one idea.

Use a supply-chain pull system (like Kanban): instead of pushing features based on roadmap guesses, install mechanisms for users to explicitly signal demand—usage analytics, feature voting, support ticket clustering. Build only what creates the strongest downstream pull signal from real workflows.

Borrow from predator-prey dynamics: treat competitor features as 'predators' and user pain points as 'prey.' Map which unmet needs have the least competitive coverage (low-predator, high-prey zones), then focus there. Use quarterly competitive sweeps to track where the ecosystem has shifted and moved.

Apply mycorrhizal network thinking: instead of deciding in isolation, map the hidden dependencies and relationships between your users, partners, and adjacent tools. Build at the intersection points where you can become a 'connector' that strengthens the whole ecosystem—high-value but non-obvious gaps.

Use a randomized A/B testing ladder: present 4-6 genuinely different feature concepts to a statistically significant user sample with minimal explanation and measure instinctive engagement (click-through, time-to-abandon, re-visit rate). Let user behavior reveal preference faster than surveys or interviews can, then rank the build queue by revealed preference.

Build a 'user intent API' that captures raw decision-making signals across all digital touchpoints (clicks, pauses, searches, abandons) and feeds them into a real-time decision engine that recommends the next feature to build before traditional surveys even close. The bold first move: instrument your entire product to emit granular behavioral data and hire a data scientist to find the hidden patterns that users can't articulate.

Create a 'reverse advisory board' where you pay 50 power users $500/month each to become your product council, meeting weekly to debate and vote on feature priorities with full transparency into your roadmap constraints and business model. The bold first move: recruit your most vocal 50 users this week, commit 10 hours/month to facilitated debates, and let them see your financials to ground their priorities in reality.

Launch a 'feature marketplace' where users propose, fund, and vote on features using a shared budget pool, so the team only builds what users collectively choose to pay for—turning feature selection into a real market signal rather than guesswork. The bold first move: allocate $50K in fictional credits, let users trade and allocate them, and commit to building the top 3 features regardless of internal preference.

Establish a 'build-in-public roadmap experiment' where the team builds 4 radically different micro-features in parallel (each taking 2 weeks), releases them all at once to different user cohorts, measures engagement velocity for 30 days, and commits to doubling down on the winner—treating your users as the ultimate arbiter through action, not opinion. The bold first move: prototype 4 contrasting ideas this sprint with skeleton teams.

Create a 'strategic partnerships fast-track' where instead of guessing what to build internally, you proactively approach your 10 most innovative customers to co-design the next major feature as a paid pilot, embedding your team inside their workflow for 6 weeks to see friction firsthand and co-own the solution. The bold first move: identify the 3 customers most likely to benefit from 10x capability and pitch them this model next week.

Deploy a 'live-decision studio' where you stream 2-hour weekly sessions of your team prototyping different solutions in real-time with rotating user guests who can instantly react, redirect, and vote on direction—turning user feedback from async and delayed into synchronous and binding. The bold first move: schedule 4 consecutive weeks of live prototype sessions and require at least one feature commit to come directly from viewer voting.

Run a 'build tax' experiment: charge users a small fee ($5-20) to propose a feature, then refund it only if the feature ships within 6 months. This filters out low-conviction requests, gives you a revenue signal on demand intensity, and creates skin-in-the-game honesty that surveys lack—ship the top 3 most-funded proposals each quarter.

Map user workflows using session replays from your 20% most-engaged users, identify the exact point where they switch to a competitor tool or manual workaround, then build the narrowest possible feature that closes that gap. Focus on behavioral abandonment points, not stated pain points—users often don't know they're leaving.

Create a 'feature decay scorecard' that tracks which existing features are used least and which correlate most with churn when absent. Rather than adding new surface area, ruthlessly cut or simplify the bottom 10% and reinvest that complexity budget into one adjacent feature that power users clearly need—build by subtraction first.

Install a 'usage cliff detector' that flags when users hit a threshold of product mastery and stop engaging (30-day inactivity after high daily use). Interview only these stalled-out power users about what blocked them next, since they've already proven they wanted value—their exit reason is more honest than onboarding feedback.

Run a monthly 'feature jury' where 12 randomly selected users are shown your actual support tickets, usage heatmaps, and competitor moves, then deliberate for 90 minutes (paid $100 each) to reach consensus on what to build. The diversity and debate forces better decisions than individual surveys, and the commitment to pay signals you're serious.

Build a 'friction flywheel' by instrumenting the exact moment users give up on a task (form abandonment, search with zero results, button click with no outcome), then automatically trigger a lightweight async follow-up asking 'what were you trying to do?' Batch these micro-confessions weekly and prioritize removing the top 5 friction points, treating completion rate as your north star.

Flip the causality: instead of asking what to build, map which features users actively *avoid* or disable after adoption, then systematically remove or invert those features. The features users delete are unambiguous signals of misalignment—build by subtraction, not addition, forcing ruthless clarity about what actually creates value.

Create a 'feature debt ledger' where every new build is treated as a loan against future user attention; users must actively re-validate each feature quarterly by opting back in or it gets sunset. This inverts the default of feature accumulation and forces continuous proof-of-value, revealing which features are genuinely needed versus which are just legacy cruft.

Establish a 'red team negation process' where half your team's job for one sprint is to argue *against* every top-voted feature request with anthropological rigor—finding the hidden assumptions, misdiagnosed problems, and second-order harms baked into user feedback. Only features that survive aggressive refutation get built.

Run a 'demand seasonality audit' that tracks which feature requests spike and disappear cyclically (by month, quarter, or business cycle), then deliberately deprioritize the spiky ones in favor of steady, evergreen requests. This surfaces which user needs are structural versus momentary, forcing you to build for the durable 80% instead of chasing the volatile 20%.

Instrument a 'feature graveyard' where you publicly archive every rejected feature request with your reasoning, then measure how often users revisit and re-advocate for the same idea—if a request keeps resurfacing from different users over months, it's a signal stronger than any single mention, revealing latent demand hidden by noise.

Deploy a 'negative option experiment' where you ship a high-demand feature to only half your user base and deliberately *hide* it from discovery for the first two weeks—measuring whether the hidden half actively searches for it versus the visible half adopts it passively. True demand pulls; passive compliance doesn't, and you'll build features that actually matter versus features users use because they're in the way.

Run a 'decision archaeology' study: interview 8-12 users who *stopped* using a competitor or abandoned your product mid-onboarding, reconstructing the exact moment and reason they quit through temporal recall. Map the decision tree that led to churn, then build the feature or fix that would have kept them—users' exit decisions reveal priorities more honestly than their stated preferences because the stakes were real enough to change behavior.

Instrument a 'feature debt ratio' metric: track which existing features have the highest support-ticket-to-usage ratio (high friction, low adoption), then allocate 40% of sprint capacity to fixing or replacing the worst offenders before building anything new. The mechanism: users won't request improvements to features they've abandoned, so fixing hidden friction unlocks latent demand that surveys will never surface.

Create a 'sequential constraint funnel': force the team to rank potential features by three orthogonal constraints (build time, user adoption ceiling, and business model fit), then systematically eliminate ideas that fail any constraint before any vote happens. This prevents the pool from being dominated by features that sound good but are trapped by hidden trade-offs—the constraint ranking itself becomes the decision mechanism.

Deploy a 'shadow roadmap' where a small sub-team builds whatever the actual users (not the vocal ones) are requesting via support tickets and dark analytics, shipping it monthly in parallel to the main roadmap. After 6 months, compare adoption and retention between main-roadmap features and shadow-roadmap features to calibrate whether the team's prioritization process is actually aligned with what moves the needle.

Run a 'workflow fragmentation audit': document the 5 most common multi-step tasks users perform across your product and adjacent tools (using screen recordings and process mining), then identify which step is the bottleneck where users pause longest or switch tools. Build only the feature that eliminates the bottleneck, since you're targeting friction that users have already accepted rather than speculative future needs.

Establish a 'commitment contract' framework where users publicly pledge (in-app or via email) which upcoming feature they would actually use, with automatic monthly reminders of their pledge; track fulfillment rate 30 days post-ship. The mechanism: users who stake their reputation on a feature request are far more likely to be telling the truth than anonymous survey respondents, and low fulfillment reveals the gap between stated and revealed preference in real time.

Borrow from evolutionary biology's concept of 'niche partitioning': segment your user base not by stated needs but by the *minimal viable feature set* each cohort requires to survive in your product. Build the feature that fills the smallest unmet niche gap—the one that lets a dormant user segment become viable—rather than optimizing for the loudest segment. Track which niches thrive or go extinct after each release.

Apply the 'tragedy of the commons' framework: identify which features or workflows are currently overused or degrading in quality (shared resources under strain), then treat feature requests as competing claims on those commons. Build the *governance mechanism* (not the feature itself) that lets users self-regulate or trade access—e.g., rate limits, usage queues, or priority auctions. Let the market reveal what users truly value by forcing them to compete for shared capacity.

Steal from particle physics: run 'feature collision experiments' where you force two seemingly unrelated user requests into the same build and measure the unexpected emergent value. Pair high-adoption features with low-adoption requests and ship them together; users often discover hidden uses at the intersection that neither group predicted. Treat collisions as feature generation events rather than roadmap conflicts.

Import the 'invasive species model' from ecology: identify which of your existing features have unexpectedly spread into use cases or user segments you never designed for. Double down on building *adjacent* capabilities that support these accidental invasions—users have already voted with behavior that this direction works, so extend it rather than chase stated demand. The most successful features often start as accidents in a different niche.

Adopt a 'negative space' approach borrowed from design criticism: instead of surveying users about what to build, map what your product *cannot* do compared to adjacent tools, then ask users to choose which gaps frustrate them most by showing them concrete workflows that fail. Present users with movie-length clips of realistic tasks that break, not abstract feature lists—this converts the impossible-to-articulate gap into a visceral choice.

Borrow from immunology's 'antigen presentation' model: when users request features, don't build them directly; instead, build a *minimal proof* (a 15-minute hacky prototype) and inject it into a small cohort's workflow for 3 days without explanation. Measure which users' immune system 'rejects' it (stops using it) versus which actively integrate it into their routine. Those who integrate it are signaling real need; those who reject it are saving you from building the wrong thing, and their rejection pattern teaches you what they actually need instead.

Run a 'capability maturity tournament' where you map each user segment onto a maturity curve (beginner → expert), then build the feature that moves the largest population segment up exactly one level—not 10x, but the narrowest bridge that scales. The bold first move: survey users on their self-assessed mastery of your core use case this week and identify which segment is clustered at the bottleneck threshold where a single feature unlocks progression for 30%+ of your base.

Instrument a 'user decision audit' that tracks not what features users click, but where they abandon workflows mid-task and what they search for next in your help docs or competitor products—the gaps between intent and resolution reveal the real problem, not the symptom. The bold first move: tag every support ticket with 'search term user tried before contacting us' and build a feature that automates the workaround they're currently doing manually.

Launch a 'inverse roadmap sprint' where the team builds 2-3 features that contradict your current user feedback, but hypothesis-test them against a small cohort with the explicit goal of learning *why* users reject them—their resistance patterns become a high-resolution map of your product's constraints and mental models. The bold first move: pick the most-requested feature you believe is wrong and intentionally ship a polarizing version to 5% of users to gather rejection rationale.

Create a 'temporal sequencing model' that maps user needs on a timeline: what do beginners need in week 1, month 1, month 6, year 1? Then identify which future-stage need is already being manually solved by early users as a workaround, and build the automation for it now—you're solving for the inevitable evolution, not the immediate complaint. The bold first move: interview 10 users who've been with you 6+ months and catalog every manual process they've created, then pick the one that would free up 5+ hours/month.

Deploy a 'revenue-locked feedback loop' where you let users pre-commit (non-binding) to paying a specific amount for a feature they vote for, then build only features with >$X in aggregated pre-commitments—combining the honesty of money with the scalability of voting. The bold first move: add a 'fund this feature' button to your public roadmap with a commitment slider and commit to building anything that hits $5K in pledges within 4 weeks.

Establish a 'shadow feature graveyard analysis' where you study every feature users built themselves as custom integrations, automations, or workarounds in their own tools (Zapier, Airtable, Sheets), then reverse-engineer the true user job from their self-built solution—the gap between what they hacked and what they asked for reveals where user intuition diverges from reality. The bold first move: survey your 50 most engaged users about what they've automated or integrated outside your product, then build the platform feature that makes their hack unnecessary.
